To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the genes identified by forward genetic screens for abnormal behaviours are expressed in neurons and affect their function and that (2) these genes are involved in the same molecular and cellular pathways that are important in other organisms.

(1) the genes required for a given behaviour are often not the genes that encode the molecules that mediate the behaviour; (2) the genes required to encode the molecules that underlie a given behaviour are not the genes that are required for that behaviour; (3) the genes required in the neurons that underly a given behaviour are the genes that are most important to that behaviour; and (4) a gene can have different roles in different neurons, and these different roles can be different

the genes we study are expressed in specific neurons, that their expression in these neurons is important for the function of these neurons, and that the function of these specific neurons is important for specific behaviours.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of genes and their products in the function of identified neurons and, ultimately, the role of these genes in behaviour.
understanding the molecular mechanisms of behaviour and how genes contribute to these mechanisms.
the identification of genes that affect behaviour, their molecular characterisation and the identification of the neurons that are responsible for the behaviour.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the study of behavioural genetics has provided a wealth of information about the genetic control of behaviour and, in turn, the behavioural control of genes.
C. elegans is the best model organism to investigate how genes affect the function of individual neurons and, through them, how they contribute to behaviour.
the worm has been used to show that a gene can be linked to a neuron and that this neuron can be implicated in behaviour.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are interested in how the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabditus elegans is wired to control behaviour.
the worm is a model for understanding how the nervous system works, and that the worm's behaviour is a model of how genes affect nervous system function.
we are trying to identify and characterise genes that are involved in the control of the feeding and egg-laying behaviours of C. elegans.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the worm is a useful model organism to study the genetic basis of behaviour.
the worm is an excellent model system for understanding how genes affect behaviour, and that the worm is also a great model for understanding how genes can be used to affect behaviour.
, in general, the genes that contribute to behaviour are the genes that are expressed in neurons.
